briefs.scd-dyspnea:
Sickle Cell Disease and Trait

trait or disease: read the electrophoresis first · what each causes · chronic dyspnea: the timing pattern picks the testIs any adult hemoglobin (HbA) present, and are the symptoms nocturnal and intermittent, or exertional and progressive?

Trait or diseaseComplicationsChronic dyspneaPractice
Bottom line
  • Sickle cell trait: HbA about 60% exceeding sickle hemoglobin (HbS) about 40%, with a completely normal complete blood count (CBC).
  • Sickle cell anemia: HbA absent; any HbA at all excludes homozygous disease (HbSS).
  • Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia: HbA present but S exceeds A, with a low mean corpuscular volume (MCV).
  • Newborn screen: FAS (fetal, adult, sickle) is trait, FS (fetal, sickle) is disease; F leads because fetal hemoglobin (HbF) predominates at birth.
  • Chronic dyspnea: nocturnal and intermittent means airway; exertional and progressive means vascular or interstitial.
  • Asthma: a common comorbidity in children and adolescents with sickle cell disease; spirometry with bronchodilator response is the first test.
Trait or disease
Hemoglobin electrophoresis: reading the pattern
ConditionElectrophoresis and CBCThe tell
NormalHbA about 97%, HbA2 (the minor adult hemoglobin) about 2.5%, HbF under 2%; normal CBCReference
Sickle cell traitHbA about 60% over HbS about 40%; completely normal CBCA exceeds S, and no anemia
Sickle cell anemiaHbA 0%, HbS about 90%; anemia, reticulocytes 10 to 20%Absent HbA is the finding
Hemoglobin SCHbA 0%, HbS about equal to hemoglobin C (HbC); milder anemiaRetinopathy and avascular necrosis out of proportion to the anemia
Sickle-beta-zero thalassemiaHbA 0%, HbS high, HbA2 elevated; low MCVLooks like HbSS but microcytic
Sickle-beta-plus thalassemiaHbA present but low, S exceeds A; low MCVThe sharpest mimic of trait
Reading it The inequality – in trait HbA always exceeds HbS, because alpha chains bind normal beta chains with higher affinity; memorize the inequality, not the numbers · HbF after infancy – under 2% by 6 months and 0 to 2% from age 2; a raised HbF later suggests hydroxyurea, a beta-thalassemia or hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin
What each one causes
Trait Painless hematuria – the most common complication: the renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic, the one microenvironment that polymerizes HbS at the 40% a carrier has; spleen, lungs and bones are spared, the vasa recta are not · Splenic infarction – real, at altitude, but uncommon · Renal medullary carcinoma – rare but nearly pathognomonic · Extreme exertion – a real risk of exertional rhabdomyolysis and sudden death, which is why trait matters in athletes and recruits
Disease only Complications – acute chest syndrome, dactylitis, stroke and osteomyelitis; none belongs to a carrier · Sepsis – pneumococcus is the leading cause despite vaccination (non-vaccine serotypes) · Osteomyelitis – Salmonella is the leading cause
Chronic dyspnea in sickle cell disease
Chronic respiratory symptoms in sickle cell disease: the differential
CauseMechanism and tellAgainst it in the night-cough case
AsthmaAirway hyperreactivity; wheeze, tightness or cough, often worse at night, with exercise or with an upper respiratory infection; normal filmThe answer: obstruction that reverses
Pulmonary hypertensionChronic hemolysis and vasculopathy; exertional dyspnea, jugular venous distension, edema, enlarged pulmonary arteriesNo edema, undisplaced apex, nocturnal rather than exertional
Pulmonary fibrosisRepeated vasoocclusive lung injury; progressive exertional dyspnea, reticular markings, honeycombing, restrictive functionNormal film; intermittent nocturnal symptoms
Pulmonary embolism (can't miss)Thrombotic risk; acute, persistent pleuritic pain and cough, tachycardia, hypoxia, raised D-dimerFour weeks, intermittent, normal vital signs
Acute chest syndrome (can't miss)Pulmonary vasoocclusion, often with infection; fever, hypoxia, chest pain, new infiltrateAfebrile, normal saturation, normal film
SarcoidosisNoncaseating granulomas, not associated with sickle cell disease; bilateral hilar adenopathyNo adenopathy; a family history is not a risk transfer
Asthma in sickle cell disease Treatment – as in anyone else: inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids · Bidirectional – acute chest syndrome drives airway hyperreactivity, and asthma raises the risk of the next acute chest syndrome, so treating it is also prevention · Clear lungs – wheezing is often absent when symptoms are mild or intermittent; spirometry with reversibility, not auscultation, is the test
Practice
  1. 17-year-old girl with homozygous sickle cell disease 4 weeks of intermittent chest tightness and dry cough worse in the middle of the night Prior acute chest syndrome; family sarcoid history Normal vital signs · lungs clear · no edema · normal chest x-ray → Spirometry with bronchodilator testing → nocturnal and intermittent means airway, so the first test is spirometry before and after a bronchodilator, looking for obstruction that reverses; clear lungs do not argue against it, since wheezing is often absent when symptoms are mild or intermittent. The angiogram answers an embolism, acute and persistent with tachycardia and hypoxia; the echocardiogram answers exertional dyspnea with right-sided failure signs. The prior acute chest syndrome makes asthma more likely, and a family history of sarcoid is not a risk transfer
  2. 1-year-old girl is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 60%, HbS 40% complete blood count normal Asymptomatic; her older sister has sickle cell anemia Afebrile · growth at the 50th percentile → Sickle cell trait → HbA exceeding HbS with a completely normal blood count is trait, not disease. Sickle cell anemia has no HbA at all; sickle-beta-plus thalassemia has HbA but S exceeds A, with a low MCV. The affected sister makes the disease complications look plausible; the most common complication of trait is painless hematuria
  3. 16-year-old boy with sickle cell disease 1 day of pleuritic chest pain chest x-ray shows a new left lower lobe infiltrate T 38.9 °C · oxygen saturation 88% on room air · HR 118/min → Transfusion with antibiotic therapy → fever, hypoxia, chest pain and a new infiltrate are acute chest syndrome, pulmonary vasoocclusion often with infection: transfuse and give antibiotics. Spirometry is for chronic, nocturnal airway symptoms, and echocardiography for exertional dyspnea with right-sided failure signs
  4. 20-year-old man with sickle cell trait nocturia and polyuria Otherwise healthy; takes no medications or diuretics urinalysis shows no glucose and no protein Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Hyposthenuria → the renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic, the one site that sickles a carrier's cells, so trait impairs urinary concentrating ability: hyposthenuria. Central diabetes insipidus is a pituitary defect; trait alone explains a medullary concentrating defect, and a normal creatinine with no protein argues against chronic kidney disease
  5. 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease exertional dyspnea jugular venous distension and pedal edema loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound No nocturnal cough or chest tightness Afebrile · HR 98/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air → Echocardiography → exertional dyspnea with right-sided failure signs is pulmonary hypertension from chronic hemolysis and vasculopathy: echocardiography shows tricuspid regurgitation with a raised estimated pulmonary pressure, and catheterization confirms. Spirometry answers nocturnal, intermittent airway symptoms, and chest computed tomography answers progressive fibrosis
  6. 1-year-old girl has laboratory results reviewed at a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 90% hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL reticulocytes 14% Parents ask what her results mean Afebrile · growth at the 25th percentile → Sickle cell anemia → no HbA with about 90% HbS, anemia and reticulocytes of 10 to 20% is sickle cell anemia: ensure penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination. Trait keeps HbA above HbS with a normal blood count, and hemoglobin SC has HbS about equal to HbC with no HbA and a milder anemia
  7. 9-month-old boy has painful swelling of the hands and feet Previously well; no recent trauma; family history unknown fingers and toes diffusely swollen and tender Afebrile · hemoglobin 7 g/dL · reticulocytes 12% → Dactylitis → painful swelling of the hands and feet is dactylitis, often the first presentation of sickle cell disease; trait carries no anemia and none of the disease complications, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis does not explain a hemoglobin of 7 with a high reticulocyte count
  8. 24-year-old woman with sickle cell disease 1 year of progressive dyspnea on exertion chest x-ray shows increased reticular markings No edema; symptoms not worse at night Afebrile · oxygen saturation 93% on room air → CT scan of the chest → progressive exertional dyspnea with reticular markings is fibrosis from repeated vasoocclusive lung injury; chest computed tomography shows honeycombing, and pulmonary function testing is restrictive. Spirometry with bronchodilator testing answers nocturnal, intermittent airway symptoms, and the pulmonary angiogram answers an acute, persistent embolism with tachycardia and hypoxia
  9. 2-year-old boy is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 15%, HbS 70% mean corpuscular volume 68 fL Parents ask whether he has sickle cell trait Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL → Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia → HbA present but S exceeding A, with a low MCV, is sickle-beta-plus thalassemia, the sharpest mimic of trait. In trait HbA exceeds HbS with a normal blood count, and sickle-beta-zero has no HbA at all
  10. 22-year-old man with sickle cell trait collapses during military basic training diffuse muscle pain and weakness dark urine Lungs clear on examination T 37.4 °C · HR 116/min · creatine kinase 48,000 U/L → Exertional rhabdomyolysis → trait carries a real risk of exertional rhabdomyolysis and sudden death under extreme exertion, which is why it matters in recruits. Acute chest syndrome belongs to disease, not to a carrier, and the lungs are clear; heat stroke alone does not fit a normal temperature
  11. 17-year-old girl with homozygous sickle cell disease 4 weeks of intermittent chest tightness and dry cough worse in the middle of the night spirometry shows airway obstruction that improves after albuterol Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air → Inhaled corticosteroid with a short-acting bronchodilator → asthma in sickle cell disease is treated as asthma is in anyone else, with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids, and control also lowers the risk of the next acute chest syndrome. Chronic transfusion does not treat reversible airway obstruction, and an oral glucocorticoid taper alone leaves out the inhaled treatment
  12. 3-year-old boy with sickle cell anemia has a high fever hypotension and tachycardia leukocytosis with bandemia Vaccinations up to date; no bone pain T 39.5 °C · BP 70/40 mm Hg · HR 168/min · leukocytes 24,000/mm3 → Streptococcus pneumoniae → pneumococcus remains the leading cause of sepsis in sickle cell disease despite vaccination (non-vaccine serotypes): start empiric ceftriaxone. Salmonella is the leading cause of osteomyelitis, and there is no bone pain; Staphylococcus aureus is not the leading septic organism
  13. 16-year-old boy has 3 months of right hip pain radiograph shows avascular necrosis of the femoral head retinopathy on dilated eye examination hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 50%, HbC 48% Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL → Hemoglobin SC disease → no HbA with HbS about equal to HbC and a milder anemia is hemoglobin SC disease, whose retinopathy and avascular necrosis run out of proportion to the anemia. Sickle cell anemia and sickle-beta-zero thalassemia both have high HbS with no HbC; the 48% HbC decides
  14. 20-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has sudden pleuritic chest pain tachycardic and short of breath at rest Chest x-ray clear; no new infiltrate Afebrile · HR 124/min · oxygen saturation 89% on room air → CT pulmonary angiogram → acute, persistent pleuritic pain with tachycardia and hypoxia and a clear film is embolism, and sickle cell disease raises thrombotic risk: computed tomography angiography shows the filling defect. Spirometry answers chronic nocturnal airway symptoms, and serum ACE answers sarcoidosis, which is not associated with sickle cell disease
  15. 19-year-old woman with sickle cell trait left upper quadrant pain began after a high-altitude flight yesterday Lungs clear; no chest pain Afebrile · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL · oxygen saturation 98% → Splenic infarction → splenic infarction is real in trait, at altitude, though uncommon. Acute chest syndrome belongs to disease, not to a carrier, and the lungs are clear; a normal hemoglobin argues against sequestration
  16. 13-year-old boy with sickle cell disease was diagnosed with asthma last year His mother asks why his asthma and his acute chest syndrome episodes each seem to raise the risk of the other Afebrile → Parenchymal hypoxia promotes inflammation and sickling within the pulmonary vasculature → parenchymal hypoxia promotes inflammation and sickling within the pulmonary vasculature, and acute chest syndrome in turn worsens airway hyperreactivity, so treating the asthma is also acute chest syndrome prevention. Hydroxyurea bronchial irritation and transfusional iron in the pulmonary vessels are not the link
  17. 2-week-old boy is seen for a weight check newborn screen reported as FAS Parents ask what the result means and whether he needs treatment Born at term; feeding well Afebrile · examination normal → Sickle cell trait → FAS is trait and FS is disease; F leads because fetal hemoglobin predominates at birth, and the A shows HbA is present, which excludes sickle cell anemia; hemoglobin SC has no HbA. Counsel the parents; no treatment
  18. 22-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has a cough chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy anterior uveitis and hypercalcemia No exertional dyspnea; symptoms not worse at night Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% → Sarcoidosis → bilateral hilar adenopathy with uveitis and hypercalcemia points to sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas); the chest film makes the diagnosis, and it is not associated with sickle cell disease, so the film decides, not the sickle history. Fibrosis shows reticular markings and honeycombing rather than hilar nodes, and asthma leaves the film normal
  19. 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has sudden pallor reticulocyte count 0.2% spleen not palpable Tired for 3 days; no jaundice or dark urine Afebrile · HR 124/min · hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL → Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis → a reticulocyte count near zero means the marrow has stopped: parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis. Splenic sequestration would bring an enlarging spleen, and hyperhemolysis would bring jaundice and dark urine with a responding marrow
  20. 28-year-old man with sickle cell trait has 2 weeks of painless hematuria imaging shows a mass in the right kidney No flank pain or fever Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg → Renal medullary carcinoma → renal medullary carcinoma is rare but nearly pathognomonic for trait; painless hematuria in a carrier is usually medullary sickling, and imaging is what excludes the carcinoma. Clear cell carcinoma is not the trait-linked tumor, and papillary necrosis makes no mass
  21. 15-year-old boy with sickle cell disease intermittent chest tightness and cough worse at night and with exercise no wheezing on examination Pulmonary function testing is ordered Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% · chest x-ray normal → Airway obstruction that reverses after bronchodilator administration → asthma is confirmed by pulmonary function testing showing airway obstruction that reverses with a bronchodilator; absent wheeze does not exclude it. A restrictive pattern belongs to fibrosis, and a low diffusing capacity with normal spirometry shows no obstruction to reverse
  22. 3-year-old girl is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 88%, HbA2 elevated mean corpuscular volume 64 fL Painful swelling of the hands at 10 months Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · reticulocytes 11% → Sickle-beta-zero thalassemia → no HbA, high HbS and a raised HbA2 with a low MCV is sickle-beta-zero thalassemia: it looks like HbSS but is microcytic. Sickle cell anemia shares the absent HbA but is not microcytic, and sickle-beta-plus keeps some HbA; the raised HbA2 decides
  23. 14-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has chest pain chest x-ray shows a new infiltrate Cough began yesterday; no leg swelling T 38.6 °C · oxygen saturation 87% on room air · HR 120/min → Acute chest syndrome → chest pain, hypoxia and a new infiltrate in sickle cell disease is acute chest syndrome, pulmonary vasoocclusion often with infection, treated with transfusion and antibiotics. Calling it pneumonia alone leaves out the transfusion, and embolism gives a clear film with a filling defect on angiography
  24. 26-year-old woman with sickle cell trait asks about future children her partner also carries sickle cell trait Neither has anemia; both have normal blood counts They plan their first pregnancy next year → 25% Disease, 50% trait, 25% unaffected → two carriers each pass a sickle gene half the time, so each pregnancy carries 25% disease, 50% trait and 25% unaffected; 50% disease overstates the risk, and not every child carries trait
  25. 14-year-old girl with sickle cell disease intermittent dry nocturnal cough for several weeks Family history of sarcoidosis; no exertional dyspnea Her parents ask which tests she needs Afebrile · lungs clear · no film yet → Serum ACE activity → serum ACE has poor sensitivity and specificity, sarcoidosis is not associated with sickle cell disease, and nothing suggests hilar adenopathy, so it should not be ordered first. The chest x-ray comes first and is expected to be normal in asthma; spirometry with bronchodilator testing then confirms
  26. 7-year-old boy with sickle cell disease develops sudden hemiparesis right arm and leg weaker than left no headache before onset Noncontrast computed tomography of the head shows no bleeding Afebrile · BP 104/62 mm Hg · glucose 92 mg/dL → Ischemic stroke → sudden hemiparesis in sickle cell disease is an ischemic stroke, a disease complication no carrier gets: treat with exchange transfusion. A scan without blood argues against hemorrhage, and no headache argues against a complicated migraine
  27. 26-year-old woman with sickle cell trait is 24 weeks pregnant 2 days of dysuria No flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness urinalysis shows leukocyte esterase and nitrites Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 88/min → Urinary tract infection → dysuria in a pregnant carrier is a urinary tract infection. Hematuria is the commonest trait complication but is painless, and pyelonephritis would bring fever and flank pain
Common wrong answers Prior acute chest syndrome, transfusions, hydroxyurea: none separates the causes of chronic dyspnea, and the prior episode makes asthma more likely, not less. Family history of sarcoidosis: no association with sickle cell disease, and no hilar nodes. Echocardiography: needs exertional dyspnea and right-sided signs; a normal point of maximal impulse and no edema argue against it. D-dimer: as with the angiogram, the picture is not embolism, so no step of that pathway applies. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy: invasive, and it answers fibrosis, already excluded. Splenic infarction as the most common trait complication: real but uncommon. An affected sibling: makes every disease complication look plausible; read the panel. Dactylitis: the disease version of the carrier stem.
Pairs with Part I Hematuria: painless hematuria, the commonest trait complication. Part II Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: the sickle cell stroke among the other pediatric causes. Part I Asthma: what follows once spirometry confirms. Part I Obstructive Lung Disease: the adult version of the which-test question.
Transferable rule

Read a supplied lab panel first; it usually excludes most of the differential in one line. A dramatic chronic disease sets the prior for its own complications but does not suspend the base rate of common disease. Ask what the timing of the complaint means before asking what the known diagnosis predisposes to.
